# Lineage {#sec-lineage}

R's oddness is not an accident that later programmers failed to clean up.
It is a hybrid engineered for interactive data analysis, afterwards asked
to carry production systems. The sophistication of the REPL and the
friction of a hardened package are the same design, seen from two ends.

## Three principles, visible from the first blackboard

In a 2016 book Chambers claimed the design of R can be summarized in three
principles. He repeated them, with the history attached, in
[*S, R, and Data Science*](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2020-028/)
(*The R Journal*, 2020). The wording there:

> objects: Everything that exists in R is an object.
>
> functions: Everything that happens in R is a function call.
>
> interfaces: Interfaces to other languages are a part of R.

He is careful about the chronology. The principles were not invented late
as a brand. They are "broadly visible from the first version of S." The
May 1976 sketch he reprints is an interface: a Fortran subroutine on one
side, an S object in, an S object out. Assignment is a function. Modeling
returns an object. The user language looks like scientific expressions
because the likely users were comfortable with scientific expressions, and
because real analyses get tree-shaped fast. A colleague's suggestion of a
shell of pipes was considered and declined. Pipes came back, decades
later, as syntax over the function-call principle. They did not replace
it.

The scalar decision is in the same essay. S had no scalar types distinct
from general objects, partly because the Fortran library already managed
arrays, partly because there were not enough programmers to build a second
language underneath. "The intention was that low-level computations
depending on these would be done through the interface to Fortran." You
are still living in that intention every time `1` is a vector.

*Extending R* (Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2016) is the book the article cites
for the principles, pages 4--11. The article is the piece you can actually
open in a browser. Prefer it when you want the history; prefer the book
when you want the design worked out as a programming model.

## A Scheme engine asked to host S

Ihaka and Gentleman's
[1996 paper](https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.1996.10474713) in the
*Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics* introduces R as a
language for data analysis and graphics, in the S tradition, with lexical
scope taken seriously. The
[R Language Definition](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-lang.html)
states the compromise in the introduction:

> The language syntax has a superficial similarity with C, but the
> semantics are of the FPL (functional programming language) variety with
> stronger affinities with Lisp and APL. In particular, it allows
> "computing on the language."

Chapter 6 of the same manual is the part to sit with. R "presents a
friendlier interface to programming than Lisp does, at least to someone
used to mathematical formulas and C-like control structures, but the
engine is really very Lisp-like." Calls are data. You can `quote` them,
rearrange them, and `eval` them. Plot labels, model formulas, and tidy
evaluation are applications of that fact. They are not a macro system
bolted on later.

What R borrowed, said plainly:

| Ingredient | Where it came from | What it still feels like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vectors as the atom, no scalars | Fortran, S, an APL-shaped semantic habit | Recycling, vectorized math, `1` having a length |
| `NA` as missingness in the runtime | S, and statistical practice | Missingness contaminates operations, on purpose |
| Attributes, lists, data frames, S3 | S | Structure without a second object heap |
| Pairlists, calls as data, `quote` / `eval` | Lisp | Metaprogramming, formulas, non-standard evaluation |
| Lexical scope, closures, first-class functions | Scheme, a deliberate break from classic S | Factories, packages as namespaces, R6-via-environment |
| A workspace and a search path | S, Bell Labs, interactive analysis | The REPL as the primary instrument |
| Generic-function OOP | S, with CLOS in the air | Verbs that live outside objects |
| Condition and restart machinery | Common Lisp, partially, and then a long cultural detour | Underused, next to `tryCatch` |
| Lazy arguments | S and R's own mix | Defaults, NSE, the pass-by-value illusion |
| Reference counts, ALTREP | R's own implementation lineage, Tierney and collaborators | Feels immutable, sometimes is not even allocated |
| A serious collector and a byte compiler | Later R core work, Tierney central to it | A runtime that can carry the illusion |

Luke Tierney's *Lisp-Stat* (Wiley, 1990) is a statistical environment built
in Lisp, with dynamic graphics and objects, and Tierney later did an
enormous share of R's runtime: the generational collector, the compiler,
reference counting, ALTREP. Influence is not identity. R is not Lisp-Stat
with different syntax. The accurate claim is smaller. The evaluator R
shipped with is Scheme-descended, and the person who then made that
evaluator industrially serious had already built a Lisp for statistics.
You can feel both facts in the dumps. You should not cite them as one
fact.

## What the corpus said

Morandat, Hill, Osvald, and Vitek,
[Evaluating the Design of the R Language](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-31057-7_6)
(ECOOP 2012), looked at the language the way language researchers look at
a language: static and dynamic analysis of a large corpus. Their abstract
is the quote to keep. R "combines lazy functional features and
object-oriented programming. This rather unlikely linguistic cocktail
would probably never have been prepared by computer scientists, yet the
language has become surprisingly popular."

The paper's lasting usefulness is the permission it gives you to treat the
cocktail as a design you can evaluate, not as weather. Lazy promises,
vectorization, a functional core, imperative locals, more than one object
system, reflection into the implementation: users pick among these ad hoc,
because the language permits all of them. That finding is still true, and
it is the reason a package has to have an opinion. The language will not
supply one.

## Interfaces, including the ones that hurt

The third Chambers principle is why `.Call`, Fortran, C++, Arrow, GDAL,
and databases do not feel like foreign-function trivia in R. They feel
like the original blackboard. The external pointer and the finalizer are
the modern picture of that 1976 rectangle: something outside, an object
on the way in, an object on the way out, and a question about who frees
the memory.

It is also why a `printf` inside that rectangle is a design bug rather
than a logging strategy. The interface was supposed to exchange objects.
Text on a C stream is a second language the caller did not agree to parse.
@sec-signals already made this point from the condition side. From the
historical side it is the same point. The interface is part of the
language, so the interface has to speak the language.

## A clash you can stop apologizing for

C-like syntax, Lisp-like engine, Fortran-like data, statistical
missingness, generic functions, and a reference-counted value illusion.
None of these is a dialect you can subtract and still have R. The work is
to know which one is speaking in a given line of code.

A `LANGSXP` is the Lisp engine. A `REALSXP` is the Fortran data. An
`ENVSXP` is the Scheme closure's home, and also R6's home. A promise is
the calling convention that makes the REPL feel telepathic. `NA` is the
statistical practice, built into the type rather than wrapped around it.
`REF` is the modern implementation earning the value illusion the syntax
has always sold. When a design argument in your package feels confused,
it is often because two of these are being asked to answer the same
question. Split the question. The lineage tells you which voice answers
which one.
